newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin rebuffs criticism of Chechnya withdrawal.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin rebuffs criticism of Chechnya withdrawal.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin defied opposition demands on Thursday that he send Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to parliament to explain the decision to withdraw Russia's last two army units from Chechnya.
Opposition parliamentarians say the pull-out amounts to acceptance of Chechen independence demands.

The opposition-dominated State Duma lower house will discuss the move at an extraordinary session on Friday. Some deputies say they might try to start impeachment moves against Yeltsin, but the chances of success were slim.

Presidential press spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing: "The president is the supreme military commander and is fully entitled to take decisions on the stationing and restationing of troops."
Yeltsin, in a letter to the Duma's communist speaker, Gennady Seleznyov, wrote that, as president, he was ultimately responsible for safeguarding Russia's territorial integrity.

He told Seleznyov he had also asked Prime Minister Chernomyrdin and the secretary of the Security Council, Ivan Rybkin, to provide a written account to deputies of all recently signed documents concerning the Chechen peace process.
That amounted to a snub of the deputies' demands for Chernomyrdin to come to the Duma personally. Lower-level representatives were due to attend the session instead.
Yeltsin's defiance was the latest gesture reasserting the 65-year-old president's authority following his heart surgery on November 5.
Interfax news agency quoted Sergei Mironov, the chief Kremlin doctor, as saying Yeltsin could start visiting the Kremlin from December 5 and resume normal work two weeks later.
"We hope that after December 15-20 Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) will be able to work at the Kremlin practically at his normal rhythm," Mironov said.
The communists, long Yeltsin's main foes, have stepped up criticism of the president and government since the operation and made the withdrawal decision the focus of their attacks.
Communist leader Genady Zyuganov, whose party has the biggest faction in the Duma, said communist deputies would meet before Friday's extraordinary session to weigh up their options.
He declined to say whether they would back calls to impeach the president or seek a no-confidence vote in the government, but appeared not to support such moves personally.
Asked if the communists would support impeachment procedures, he said: "The president is ill, let him get well."
Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais, talking to reporters during a visit to St Petersburg, said the communists' attacks were "completely absurd".

"Just over a year ago some Duma deputies initiated impeachment procedures over the sending of troops to Chechnya. Today they are talking about impeachment for withdrawing the troops from Chechnya," he said.

Tens of thousands of people, mainly civilians, have been killed in the Chechnya conflict. Fighting largely halted under a ceasefire last August but no solution has been found to the central dispute over Chechnya's status -- in or out of Russia.
